tagline: Build a content brief by scraping and comparing a handful of competitor pages you point it at.
verdictSummary: Fetching a handful of user-supplied competitor URLs, extracting their headings and word counts, and assembling a structured brief (target topics, common subheadings, rough length target) is a genuine one-sitting build with no ongoing infrastructure. What it cannot replicate is Clearscope's actual data source: live search-engine ranking data across millions of keywords, which is what tells you which competitors to even look at in the first place.
coreLoopDIY: Fetch and parse a handful of user-supplied competitor URLs, extract their heading structure and approximate word count, and assemble a brief listing common subtopics, a target length range, and terms that appear across most of the pages.
whatYouLose: live keyword and SERP ranking data to identify which competitors actually rank, rather than ones you guess and paste in
a proprietary content-grading score correlated against real ranking outcomes
continuous monitoring that re-scores content as rankings shift over time
CMS and workflow integrations for a content team
agency-grade reporting to show a client
whyPeopleStillPay: People pay for Clearscope because knowing which pages to analyze in the first place requires real-time search ranking data — without it, you're pasting in URLs you already guessed matter, not the ones search engines actually show for that query. The subscription buys that ranking visibility and a score correlated against real outcomes, not just the page-parsing step after it.
prompt:
Build a local content-brief generator: fetch a handful of user-supplied competitor URLs and assemble a structured brief from what's actually on those pages. Stack: Python, Playwright for rendering JavaScript-heavy pages, no database needed — this runs as a one-shot CLI or local script per brief, not a persistent service.

Core loop: the user pastes in 3–8 competitor URLs for a topic they already researched separately. The tool fetches and renders each page, extracts the heading structure (H1–H3), approximate word count, and a simple term-frequency pass over the body text. It then assembles a brief: subtopics that appear as headings across most of the pages, a target word-count range based on the competitor average, and a list of terms that show up frequently across sources — presented as raw signal for a human writer to interpret, not a score to chase.

Requires only permission to fetch the URLs the user provides — no API key, no ongoing hosting. State plainly that URL selection is entirely manual: this tool has no way to know which pages actually rank for a query, only what's on the pages you hand it.

Do not build: live SERP scraping to auto-discover competitor URLs (that's a legal and technical undertaking well beyond this tool's scope, and Google's terms explicitly prohibit it), a content-quality score claiming correlation with rankings, or continuous re-monitoring — this produces one brief from one batch of URLs, not an ongoing dashboard.

faq.q: Can I import my existing Clearscope briefs?
faq.a: Clearscope lets you export a brief's term list and outline as text, which you can reference manually, but there's no automated import — this tool generates its own briefs from URLs you supply, not from Clearscope's stored ones.

faq.q: Will it work on my phone?
faq.a: As a CLI or a very simple local web page, it's not built with mobile in mind — pasting in URLs and reading the resulting brief works better on a larger screen.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: Nothing beyond hosting or running it locally — there's no API to pay for, since it's just fetching pages you point it at and doing local text analysis.

faq.q: What's the one thing that doesn't survive the rebuild?
faq.a: Knowing which competitors to look at. Clearscope tells you who's actually ranking for a keyword right now; this tool has no ranking data at all, so choosing the right URLs to analyze is entirely on you, and a bad choice there means a misleading brief no matter how good the parsing is.
